title: Conscious possession - the most litigated phrase in NDPS cases
p1:
A person found near contraband is not always automatically guilty.

The phrase that often decides the fate of NDPS cases is not just “possession” — it is “conscious possession.”
p2:
Many assume that if a prohibited substance is found nearby, conviction is certain. But the law asks a deeper question: Did the person know about it and have control over it?

A surprising point is that physical custody alone may not be enough. The prosecution often has to establish awareness and the ability to exercise control over the substance.
p3:
In simple words, finding something with a person is different from proving that the person knowingly possessed it.

This distinction has made “conscious possession” one of the most debated and frequently argued phrases in NDPS litigation. It reminds us that criminal liability depends not only on what is found, but also on what can be proved.

The practical takeaway: in NDPS matters, facts like location, ownership, knowledge, and circumstances around recovery can become crucial.
conclusion: Do you think mere physical possession should be enough for conviction, or should the law always require proof of knowledge and control?
